title: The Philokalia (1782)
hookLine: two Greek monks gather the Orthodox writings on inner prayer into one collection

cards: Advice from desert hermits. Notes from abbots on watching your thoughts. Short teachings on how to keep praying while you work, walk and eat.
For generations, monks copied these out by hand, and they sat scattered across monastery libraries, in manuscripts few people could ever see.
Then two monks decide it should all be in one place, printed, where anyone who wanted it could find it. They give their anthology a name that sounds less like a manual than a love letter.

teach.b: The two monks were Nikodemos of the Holy Mountain, from Mount Athos, and Makarios of Corinth, a bishop.
Their book gathers writings by Orthodox teachers across the centuries on what the Orthodox call watchfulness: guarding the heart, noticing thoughts as they arrive, and praying inwardly.
The title is Greek, and it carries our line: Philokalia, love of the beautiful, or love of the good. The beautiful here isn't a painting. It's God, and a heart made quiet enough to love God.
At the center of much of the book is a very short prayer, the Jesus Prayer.
Orthodox Christians pray it in words like these: Lord Jesus Christ, Son of God, have mercy on me. It grows out of the Gospels.
In Luke, a blind man by the road near Jericho calls out, "Jesus, thou Son of David, have mercy on me."
And in Jesus's parable the tax collector stands far off in the temple and prays only, "God be merciful to me a sinner."
Paul tells the Thessalonians: "Pray without ceasing." How do you do that?

You give the mind one short prayer, said slowly, often with the breath, until it's less something you say and more something the heart keeps saying. The writers are honest that this isn't a technique for calm.
They warn against chasing experiences, and they say a beginner needs a guide. Catholics have their own long tradition of contemplative prayer, and some Protestants pray short breath prayers too.
But this collection comes from the Orthodox, and the way of prayer it teaches is theirs.

how: Orthodox Christians may pray the Jesus Prayer with a prayer rope, a cord of knots, saying the prayer once on each knot, ideally under the guidance of a priest or spiritual father or mother.

games.q: you're a monk on the Holy Mountain. the old teachings on inner prayer are scattered in manuscripts few can read. what do you do?
o: keep them safely in the library.
gather them into one book and print it.
write a new teaching of your own.
games.why: Nikodemos and Makarios gathered them into one printed anthology and named it Philokalia, love of the beautiful.

practice: Sit still and let your breathing slow. If you pray, say the Jesus Prayer silently, Lord Jesus Christ, Son of God, on the in-breath, have mercy on me, on the out-breath, and when your mind wanders, come back without fuss.
If you don't pray, simply breathe, and on each out-breath let the word mercy pass through.

wordCard.voice: Philokalia. A Greek word meaning love of the beautiful, and the name of an Orthodox anthology on inner prayer and watchfulness of the heart.
